default.p.test-44-p1.vietnamese:
As advances in medicine, improvements in living conditions, and better eating habits have lengthened human life spans, the population continues to grow. If this continues, however, we may be unable to secure enough food resources to support that population. Fish species that were once caught in large quantities are beginning to disappear, and the number of organisms becoming extinct is also increasing.

In Japan, severe El Niño conditions have occurred in recent years, and warm winters have continued for long periods. Not only in Japan but all over the world, "abnormal" weather phenomena are occurring.

There is a risk that even more serious events will occur in the future. Sea levels in Tokyo Bay are said to be rising, and in the near future the cities along the bay may be submerged.

If we use enormous amounts of energy to mass-produce goods, consume them, and continually throw them away, the economy will indeed run smoothly. We have been operating according to this logic, but if we continue in this way, the coexistence and survival of the Earth's diverse forms of life will be endangered. We must quickly shift to a way of life that produces only what is necessary, using as little energy as possible, and disposes of waste.

Transporting raw materials and fuel to factories to mass-produce goods, and then transporting the finished products everywhere, consumes enormous amounts of energy. However, if each household makes by hand the things that can be made at home, energy consumption will be greatly reduced.

Should we not reconsider the value of the handmade world once again? For example, if we try to grow as many of the vegetables we eat as possible, the energy used for production and distribution will be significantly reduced, while healthy agriculture can be practiced without relying on the pesticides or artificial fertilizers used in mass production. At the very least, for the fruits and vegetables we ourselves eat, anyone would want to grow them without pesticides or chemical fertilizers, and that is entirely possible.

In the past, people did not have as much money as we do today, yet they lived happily in their own way. Because they made many things themselves and supported one another, money was not as necessary as it is now. Having more money and being able to buy everything does not necessarily make people happy.

Minimize the waste of resources and produce only what is truly necessary. And adopt a lifestyle that thoroughly cares about and prioritizes the environment. I believe this is the age in which we must seriously consider making that a reality.

（Note 1）食糧: Same meaning as 食料

（Note 2）El Niño: A phenomenon in which sea-surface temperatures rise, causing abnormal weather on a global scale

default.p.test-48-p1.vietnamese:
In one of my classes, after speaking for about an hour, I suddenly said: 「Now, please summarize everything I have talked about so far in two minutes without leaving out any of the main points」. Almost everyone reacted: 「I didn't hear anything about that. Being told to do this out of nowhere is too difficult」. They frantically said to one another: 「If I'd known, I would have taken notes from the beginning」.

Twenty percent of the students took careful notes from the very beginning without being told to do so, while the remaining eighty percent merely stared blankly as if thinking, 「Oh, the teacher is giving a lecture」. These eighty percent became flustered, saying: 「Everything is completely different from how it was at the beginning」.

This does not mean that these eighty percent had failed to listen to the lecture. On the contrary, subjectively speaking, I believe they were all convinced that they had listened attentively. I had not said anything particularly difficult, so while listening, they must have assumed that they understood everything. However, when asked to accurately reproduce what they had taken in, they were completely unable to do so. As a natural result, they felt: 「Everything is completely different from what I imagined」.

A similar phenomenon can also be found in everyday life. For example, suppose someone teaches you how to operate a computer. When the instructor explains that you should move this way and follow this sequence, you may feel that you have a rough understanding of it. Have you ever said, 「I understand. Thank you very much」, but then forgotten every step and found your mind completely blank when you actually tried to perform the operation yourself, as if you had never known it?

If you take notes while receiving the explanation, you can look at those notes and reproduce the operation once again. Therefore, when you have to explain again what you heard from someone else, the most essential ability is note-taking. Developing the habit of taking notes is the most important thing.

The reason people cannot reproduce a computer operation even though they are convinced that they understood it is that certain parts are omitted from the instructor's explanation. Instructors are experienced and so accustomed to using computers that they press certain keys as a matter of course. For example, when turning on the power, they do not imagine that someone might not know how to do it, so they leave it out of the explanation. Many actions go unexplained in this way. However, unless the listener also takes notes on these details, they will never be able to do the operation independently.

（Note 1）Input: putting information inside

（Note 2）Output: sending information outside

（Note 3）Instructor: someone who teaches or provides technical guidance

default.p.test-49-p2.vietnamese:
「See you over there」「Please take care of me over there, too」. Yesterday morning, as I walked around Tokyo's Tsukiji Market, I heard words like these. They meant that the speakers hoped to continue their business relationship at Toyosu, where the market would be moving. They must have been regular customers greeting and chatting with one another.▼
The variety and abundance of the shops here, as well as the beauty of their displays…… The cultural anthropologist Lévi-Strauss was the one who described Tsukiji as「equal to all the museums in the world」. The market that once drew so many people simply for the pleasure of viewing its countless varieties of seafood now has only today's and tomorrow's auctions left.▼
Our company is located in Tsukiji; we could almost say it is right next door. Whenever I was stuck for ideas while writing a draft and looked out the window, Tsukiji Market was always in view. That familiar scene is about to become something「that once existed in the past」. But then I reconsidered: after all, the「outer market (Jogai)」that serves delicious fresh fish is not going to disappear.▼
The outer market, adjacent to Tsukiji Market, began as a shopping district and has now become a lively food street visited by tourists from overseas. When I first heard the slogan「Even if Tsukiji moves, the outer market will remain」, I was quite surprised, but thinking about it, a neighborhood would naturally continue to exist and develop in this way.▼
Kanda in Tokyo, where many bookstores and publishing houses are concentrated, was originally the location of the predecessors of the University of Tokyo and Hitotsubashi University. When students gathered there, demand for books arose, and even after the universities moved elsewhere, the area continued to be a neighborhood of books. Perhaps Tsukiji, too, will develop further as a neighborhood of fish.▼
This was a relocation repeatedly delayed after a long series of debates over safety. The familiar name「Uogashi (Fish Wharf)」of Tsukiji Market will surely be passed on to Toyosu. Along with the lively atmosphere created by the professionals who support Japan's culinary culture.

（Note 1）Tsukiji Market: A fish market in Tsukiji, Tokyo. It moved to Toyosu in 2018

（Note 2）Regular customer: A customer who frequently visits a particular shop

（Note 3）Equal to: Having equivalent value

（Note 4）Countless: A great many; innumerable

（Note 5）Seri: Selling goods in an auction-like manner

（Note 6）Our company: The company where the writer works

（Note 7）Predecessor: The earlier form of an organization before it became what it is today

default.p.test-5-p1.vietnamese:
The Japanese giant salamander is the largest amphibian in the world, and large individuals exceed 1.5 meters in total length. Because it has barely evolved since about 30 million years ago, it is called a 「living fossil」. In Japan today, it lives in rivers west of Gifu Prefecture.

Because the Japanese giant salamander is nocturnal, it remains still beneath large rocks during the day. At night, it moves quickly through the water and eats small fish, crabs, insects, and other creatures. Because its eyes are not very well developed, it rarely chases prey. Instead, when prey comes directly in front of it, it snaps it up. Therefore, if you bring your face or hand close in front of its eyes, it may mistake you for prey and bite you, making this extremely dangerous.

（Note 1）Japanese giant salamander: A large amphibian found only in Japan

（Note 2）Amphibian: A creature that breathes through gills when young and through lungs when fully grown

（Note 3）Nocturnal behavior: The habit of resting during the day and being active at night

default.p.test-5-p2.vietnamese:
Haiku is a uniquely structured Japanese poetic form consisting of seventeen sounds in a five–seven–five rhythm. Haiku basically contains a "kigo," or seasonal word. Kigo are words associated with the seasons, and including one makes it easy to understand the scene depicted in the haiku. However, because customs associated with kigo may differ between the past and the present, and because kigo are classified according to the lunar calendar, they may sometimes seem out of step with the season we imagine.

For example, the "swing," which is now used year-round as a toy, became a spring kigo because it was once used at spring festivals in ancient China. Also, although morning glories bloom in summer, August, when morning glories bloom, is autumn according to the lunar calendar, so they became an autumn kigo.

Once you know the background and origins of kigo, haiku containing them become deeper and more moving. You will also surely be inspired to recognize the beauty of the four seasons. When reading haiku, if a kigo catches your attention or makes you curious, be sure to look into it carefully.

（Note 1）Custom: A way of life passed down from ancient times

（Note 2）Lunar calendar: A calendar used in Japan before 1872

（Note 3）Background: The situation or circumstances underlying a thing or event

（Note 4）Origin: The source from which something began

default.p.test-50-p1.vietnamese:
— What prompted you to start writing novels?

This is undoubtedly the question I am asked most often in magazine and newspaper interviews. Although I can state this with complete confidence, I think most people who write are fed up with questions like this.

Naturally, I am no exception. At first, I would rack my brain to choose my words and try to come up with a suitably impressive answer. But after being in the public eye for a while and becoming accustomed to interviews and gathering material, I would either give a perfunctory answer just to get it over with or force the conversation to an end by saying, “Nothing prompted me at all.” There was even a period when I would casually spin out made-up stories, improvising them on the spot as though they were true.

If the question “What prompted you to start writing novels?” means “Why did you become a novelist?”, then in my case the answer is very simple. It was because I (fortunately) received a newcomer’s award from a literary magazine.

However, if “What prompted you to start writing novels?” is meant literally—that is, “Why do you write novels?”—then I think “Nothing prompted me at all” is the most honest answer.

Suppose, for example, that you received a love letter. Would anyone ask the person who wrote it, “Hey, what made you feel like writing a love letter?” The person being asked would surely be taken aback by the tactlessness of the question and think to themselves, “Why would you ask something like that?”

（Note 1）この手の: of this kind, this type

（Note 2）類い: things of a similar nature, things of the same kind

（Note 3）出まかせ: irresponsible words that come out spontaneously and arbitrarily

default.p.test-55-p1.vietnamese:
Whether language use is an exclusive privilege of humans is not entirely beyond doubt. Zoologists have observed species such as sticklebacks, gulls, and, especially, apes closely related to humans, and discovered that processes very similar to human language are also taking place in the worlds of these animals. The more reports of such discoveries people read, the more inclined they become to think that perhaps the difference between animal "language" and human language is merely a difference of degree. Yet even if it is a difference of degree, there still appears to be a vast gap between the language humans use and animal language.

This is because, by using language with one another, humans can "understand" one another. Animal societies also display phenomena resembling language, but animals entirely lack the function that enables humans to "understand" one another through language. What exists in the animal world—especially among lower animals—is merely a set of almost instinctive responses to specific stimuli, not the mechanism of "understanding" that operates between humans.

So what, after all, does "understanding" mean? The notion of "empathy," often discussed by psychologists, may provide one useful clue when considering this question.

For example, let us consider the relationship between a doctor and a patient. The patient explains that a particular part of the body hurts. The person tells the doctor that the affected area "hurts." When the doctor hears the word "pain," a process takes place within him. The doctor uses his own experience to imagine a state similar to the bodily condition that the patient is expressing through the word "pain."

The doctor does not necessarily feel pain in that particular part of his own body. Nevertheless, he knows what kind of bodily state the patient is trying to express through the word "pain."

（Note 1）Lower animals: Animals considered to have a lower level of evolution and simpler body structures.

（Note 2）Instinctive: Having that quality innately.

（Note 3）Affected area / injured area: The part of the body affected by an illness or injury.

（Note 4）Based on / in accordance with: Applying something to or comparing it against a particular standard.

default.p.test-56-p1.outline.2.label: Japanese open architecture and harmony with nature
default.p.test-56-p1.outline.2.note: Unlike the two regions described above, Japanese homes are open because of the mild climate and beautiful four seasons; from architecture to cuisine, they are closely connected with nature.
default.p.test-56-p1.outline.3.label: Why Japanese people favor wood and the concept of impermanence
default.p.test-56-p1.outline.3.note: Explains that the deeper reason Japanese people favor wood is the Buddhist concept of impermanence and respect for the natural cycle of creation and destruction. Passage supporting Question 2.

default.p.test-56-p1.vietnamese:
When it comes to floor coverings, Persian carpets are so famous that people immediately think of them. Yet it is strangely hard to understand why such beautiful floral patterns came to be created on carpets in that desolate desert. I nodded in understanding when a certain expert told me the following story.

In that region, spring arrives for only about three short weeks each year, and the land becomes a flower-filled paradise so beautiful that it awakens people in amazement. Once that period has passed, everything returns to a monotonous world of sand and sky. To preserve spring forever in their homes, people made flowers bloom on their floors, and this is said to have been the origin of carpets. I was truly impressed and felt that this was exactly the kind of story one could never understand without visiting the place oneself.

When looking at textiles made in Northern Europe, one is struck by their surprisingly bright pastel colors, and this too must have arisen from a similar environment. For only three months of the year, spring, summer, and autumn arrive together; then the long, cold, dark winter begins, confining people indoors. The image of spring longed for by people spending the winter shut inside their “nests” must surely be none other than those brilliantly glowing pastel colors. Seen in this way, I feel I can understand the secret behind the bright, beautiful colors created in Northern Europe.

Compared with these regions, Japanese homes are open and airy. Whether shinden-zukuri, shoin-zukuri, or sukiya-zukuri, the reason such open housing took shape and became established in Japan is that the climate is mild: the summer heat and winter cold are not too severe, the four seasons change distinctly, and nature generously offers beauty at every moment. It was from the desire to welcome these things into daily life that a deep harmony with nature began. As living spaces gradually settled into this form, places in direct contact with nature, such as the eaves and engawa verandas, became increasingly important. The dishes enjoyed there also incorporated the seasons. Japanese cuisine is often arranged like a miniature garden reflecting the natural landscape, and that is why nature is so strongly reflected even in food.

To build such houses, wood is the most suitable material. However, I believe there is another reason Japanese people favor wood: the Buddhist view of impermanence. Our ancestors realized that both nature and society are constantly changing. Living in accordance with this natural law, without resisting it, is the Japanese way of life. Because they believed that all things, like human life, are brief and limited, they may have felt spiritually drawn to wood—a material that decays and returns to the natural earth.

(Note 1) Kōryō-taru: desolate, bare, and lonely

(Note 2) Saru: a certain, some

(Note 3) Hokuō: Northern Europe—the countries in the northern part of Europe

(Note 4) Fuyugomori: wintering—the act of people or animals staying indoors or in their nests throughout winter

(Note 5) Machikogareru: to long for—to eagerly and intensely yearn for

(Notes 6, 7, 8) Shinden-zukuri, Shoin-zukuri, Sukiya-zukuri: traditional Japanese residential architectural styles

(Note 9) Nokisaki, Engawa: an open space between the interior of a room and the outdoors in a traditional Japanese house

(Note 10) Mujōkan: the view of impermanence—the belief that nothing is unchanging or eternal

(Note 11) Kuchite: to decay—to rot and break down into pieces

A

Subject: Invitation to Give a Lecture

Dear Professor Kazuhiro Yamamoto, Department of △△, ○○ University,

Greetings. My name is Kyoko Takeda from the General Affairs Department of Aqua Co., Ltd. This is my first time contacting you.
Please forgive me for the discourtesy of suddenly sending you this email.

Our company is planning to hold a training seminar aimed at expanding our business overseas in the future.
We are writing to earnestly invite you, Professor Yamamoto, who teaches at a university while also actively researching the constantly changing international situation, to give a lecture at the seminar.
We would be grateful if you would consider accepting our invitation under the following conditions.

Date and time: Friday, October 20, 20XX, 18:00–19:30
Venue: ABC Convention Hall—Small Hall
Topic: 「Southeast Asian Economy」
Participants: Approximately 120
Honorarium: ¥300,000

We realize that you are very busy and feel truly apologetic for imposing on you, but we would greatly appreciate it if you could let us know a schedule that would be convenient for you.
Thank you very much for your consideration.

==================================================
Aqua Co., Ltd.
General Affairs Department: Kyoko Takeda
Address: Orient Building 12F, 8-16 △△ Street, ○○ Ward, Tokyo
Phone: 03-XXXX-XXXX | Fax: 03-XXXX-XXXX
Email: k-takeda@aqua.co.jp
==================================================

B

Subject: Update on Current Situation & Notice of Lecture Venue Change

Dear Professor Kazuhiro Yamamoto, Department of △△, ○○ University,

We sincerely thank you for your continued support.
We would also like to thank you again for kindly accepting our invitation to give a lecture the other day.

In the hope that as many employees as possible would have the opportunity to hear your insights in person, we contacted our affiliated companies as well. As a result, the number of registrations from both our company and our affiliated companies has far exceeded our initial expectations.
Since this is a rare opportunity, we would be grateful for your approval to move the lecture to a larger hall so that all interested employees can attend.
In addition, we would like to ask your permission to set aside an additional 30 minutes for a question-and-answer session after the lecture.

We sincerely apologize for this sudden request, but we ask for your understanding and approval.

(Before the change) ABC Convention Hall—Small Hall | Participants: Approximately 120
(After the change) ABC Convention Hall—Medium Hall | Participants: Approximately 300
~ (The following has been omitted)

(Note 1) 弊社 (heisha): Our company; a humble way of referring to one's own company

(Note 2) 教鞭をとる (kyouben o toru): To teach students or pupils

default.p.test-6-p1.outline.0.label: Definition of an invasive species
default.p.test-6-p1.outline.0.note: Defines an invasive species as a species that did not originally exist in an area but was brought there from elsewhere.
default.p.test-6-p1.outline.1.label: Example 1: European bumblebee
default.p.test-6-p1.outline.1.note: Explains the importation of foreign bees for greenhouse agriculture and the negative consequences when they escape into the wild (reducing native bee populations through competition for food and nesting sites and interfering with pollination). Main evidence for Question 1.
default.p.test-6-p1.outline.2.label: Example 2: Red-eared slider
default.p.test-6-p1.outline.2.note: Explains that imported red-eared sliders kept as pets are released into the wild by their owners, where competition reduces native turtle populations and disrupts the ecosystem of ponds and lakes. Question 2 is based mainly on this section.
default.p.test-6-p1.outline.3.label: Overall effects and preventive measures
default.p.test-6-p1.outline.3.note: The passage summarizes the diverse harm caused by invasive species to ecosystems, people, and agriculture, and calls for following three principles to prevent damage.
default.p.test-6-p1.outline.4.label: Vocabulary and terminology notes
default.p.test-6-p1.outline.4.note: The passage explains six technical terms appearing in the reading: European bumblebees, agricultural greenhouses, native species, competition, red-eared sliders, and ecosystems.
default.p.test-6-p1.vietnamese:
Invasive species are organisms that did not originally exist in a particular area but were introduced from other regions.

① European bumblebees were imported in the 1990s for use in greenhouse cultivation of tomatoes. However, European bumblebees that escaped from the greenhouses became wild in the natural environment. As a result, they are reducing the population of native bumblebees by competing with them for food and nesting sites. In addition, they have a habit of biting the lower parts of flowers to suck out nectar, which interferes with plant pollination.

② Red-eared sliders were imported as pets from the latter half of the 1950s. Red-eared sliders that had been kept as pets were abandoned and became wild. They then competed with native turtles, such as Japanese pond turtles and striped-neck turtles living in the same ponds, reducing their populations. Furthermore, by eating fish, insects, flowers, and grasses, they are disrupting the balance of pond and lake ecosystems.

Thus, when invasive species become established in the wild, they have various effects on Japan's ecosystems. In addition, invasive species are causing damage to human lives and bodies as well as to agriculture.

To prevent damage caused by invasive species, people are calling for the following: do not bring any more invasive species into Japan, do not abandon invasive species being kept, and do not increase the populations of invasive species that are already present.

(Note 1) Seiyou oomaruhana-bachi: A species of bumblebee native to Europe

(Note 2) Vinyl house: An agricultural greenhouse covered with vinyl sheeting

(Note 3) Native species: Plants and animals originally found in a particular area

(Note 4) Competition: Competing or contending with one another

(Note 5) Red-eared slider: A species of turtle native to the Americas...

(Note 6) Ecosystem: The whole set of relationships among organisms and their surrounding environment

default.p.test-7-p1.outline.2.label: A tactful communication strategy for expressing an opposing opinion.
default.p.test-7-p1.outline.2.note: Advises minimizing negative wording and using gentler expressions so that discussions can progress constructively
default.p.test-7-p1.vietnamese:
During discussions or meetings, have you ever unintentionally said what you wanted to say while rejecting the other person's opinion? For example: "The location Mr. A suggested is not good. It will be a problem when it rains, so it would be better to stay indoors." How would Mr. A feel upon hearing this? He would probably be angry, thinking, "I went to the trouble of making a suggestion, so why did they have to put it that way?"

When proposing an opinion different from someone else's, if we remember to avoid negative wording as much as possible—for example, "The location Mr. A suggested is also good. However, considering the possibility of rain, wouldn't it be better to stay indoors?"—we can conduct discussions more effectively.

default.p.test-7-p2.outline.0.note: The passage explains that rice fields support many living creatures because nutrients in the soil create food chains, while moderate human intervention allows many species to coexist.

default.p.test-7-p2.outline.1.note: The passage introduces Aotakaze, a wind blowing across rice fields, and explains how water evaporation lowers the surrounding air temperature compared with that of urban areas. It provides evidence for Question 2.
default.p.test-7-p2.outline.2.label: The roles of rice fields and awareness of environmental protection

default.p.test-7-p2.outline.3.label: Notes on specialized terminology
default.p.test-7-p2.outline.3.note: Definitions of two terms in the passage: microorganisms (微生物) and evaporation (蒸発).
default.p.test-7-p2.vietnamese:
Many living organisms inhabit rice paddies. This is because nutrients in the paddy soil support numerous microorganisms. Insects that feed on these microorganisms then gather there, followed by organisms that feed on those insects. In addition, the regular human intervention involved in bringing water to the same place at the same time every year, planting rice, weeding, harvesting, and so on prevents only certain strong species from surviving. In other words, even weaker organisms can survive, and as a result, many diverse species are able to live together.

Furthermore, the breeze blowing over fields where the rice is growing lush and green is cool and refreshing. This breeze is called「①Aotakaze (green field breeze)」. When water vapor evaporates from the surface of a rice paddy into the air, it takes heat away from its surroundings. The air is cooled at this time, reducing the heat around the rice paddy, which is why the breeze blowing over it becomes cool. Some studies have also found that areas around rice paddies have lower temperatures than urban areas.

In addition to serving as places where rice—the staple food that sustains us—is produced, rice paddies can be said to have ②many other different roles, and both people and other plants and animals are benefiting from them. From now on, it is extremely important to continue protecting environments that contain rice paddies.

(Note 1) Microorganism: An extremely tiny living organism

(Note 2) Evaporation: The process by which water changes into a gas

default.p.test-7-p3.outline.0.label: The origin and spread of postage stamps
default.p.test-7-p3.outline.0.note: Introduces the history of postage stamps, created in Britain about 180 years ago to simplify postage calculations, then quickly adopted worldwide and issued in Japan in 1871.
default.p.test-7-p3.outline.1.label: The nature of replacing money and techniques for preventing stamp counterfeiting
default.p.test-7-p3.outline.1.note: Explains that a stamp is proof that a fee has been paid, serving as a substitute for money (evidence for Question 4), and describes sophisticated anti-counterfeiting printing techniques such as hidden printing and holograms.
default.p.test-7-p3.outline.2.label: The meaning of postmarks and the pleasure of collecting them
default.p.test-7-p3.outline.2.note: The passage introduces postmarks (消印), explains their two main purposes, which provide the evidence for Question 5, and describes the hobby of collecting unique seasonal or regional postmarks.
default.p.test-7-p3.outline.3.label: Notes on specialized vocabulary
default.p.test-7-p3.outline.3.note: Explains the specialized terms noted in the passage: watermark pattern (すかし模様) and distinctive characteristic (特殊).
default.p.test-7-p3.vietnamese:
Postage stamps were first issued in Britain about 180 years ago. Because calculating postage according to differences in distance and the weight of mail was difficult, stamps were devised as a substitute for postal fees. Thanks to this convenience, postage stamps quickly spread throughout the world. In Japan, postage stamps were first issued in 1871.

A postage stamp is affixed to mail as proof that the postage has been paid. In other words, it is ① a substitute for money. Therefore, various improvements were devised to make it impossible to produce identical imitations. In the early days of stamps, they were printed with embossed designs added to the paper. Before long, a distinctive method of printing stamps with holographic film—a film that changes color and appearance depending on the angle of the light—also began to be used.

After mail is collected, a post office places a mark called a "postmark" on the stamp, showing the name of the post office and the date and time. Applying a "postmark" has ② two purposes. One is to indicate the name of the post office that accepted the mail, together with the date and time; the other is to prevent a stamp that has already been used from being reused. Seasonal or regional limited-edition marks are sometimes applied as well, so there are people who collect stamps not only to enjoy the stamps themselves but also these postmarks.

（Note 1） Embossed design (watermark-like pattern): A design that becomes visible when held up toward the light

（Note 2） Distinctive: Different from the ordinary

default.p.test-8-p1.vietnamese:
Many people think that, when it comes to themselves, they are the ones who understand themselves best. However, everyone has aspects of themselves that they do not recognize. When people around us point out good and bad qualities that we have not noticed, being told about our good qualities feels pleasant and is surely something that makes us happy. On the other hand, regarding our bad qualities, we may be shocked because such comments are difficult to hear and painful. Nevertheless, if we can honestly accept criticism about our weaknesses, our problems and areas for improvement will become clear, and this will certainly help us grow.

(Note 1) 耳が痛い: Difficult or painful to hear.

default.p.test-8-p2.vietnamese:
With the spread of the Internet and social networking services (SNS), necessary information has become easy to obtain, making our lives more convenient. Whenever we want to know the meaning of an unfamiliar word or the route to a destination, we can look it up immediately. However, this information includes many different kinds: accurate information, unreliable information, and dangerous information. At times, we may also become confused by the overwhelming amount of information. When receiving information, it is essential to have the judgment needed to decide which information to trust and accept.

At the same time, individuals have more opportunities to freely transmit information through social media. However, misunderstanding how to share information can also cause trouble. When transmitting information ourselves, we must carefully check whether it is inaccurate, whether its wording could be misleading, and whether it reveals personal information. In addition, even if we assume that we are sending information only to family or friends, it may still be seen by a large number of unspecified people. Furthermore, once information has been posted on the Internet, it cannot be completely erased if it spreads. In light of these points, it is extremely important to take responsibility for the information we transmit.

（Note 1）SNS: Social Networking Service. A type of service on the Internet

（Note 2）普及: The spread of something to the general public

（Note 3）個人情報: Information about a person that could make that individual’s identity recognizable

（Note 4）細心: Paying careful attention even to the smallest details

（Note 5）不特定多数の人の目に触れる: To be seen by a large number of unspecified people

（Note 6）拡散: The act of spreading or expanding

default.p.test-9-p1.outline.4.note: Explain the terms marked with footnote numbers: damaged packaging, excess inventory, best-before date, and expiration date.
default.p.test-9-p1.vietnamese:
Have you ever heard the term “food waste”? Food waste refers to food that is thrown away even though it is still edible. In Japan, the amount of food wasted in a year is said to reach 5 to 9 million tons.

One initiative proposed as a way to reduce food waste is called a Food Bank. A food bank collects food that is about to be thrown away and provides it to people who need food. This initiative began in the United States in 1967 and started in Japan after 2000.

Food banks do not accept and process every kind of food. They accept food that is still edible but would otherwise be discarded for reasons such as damaged packaging or excessive inventory. Items such as boxed meals and sandwiches cannot be accepted because the period between their sell-by date and use-by date is short.

Using food banks benefits both the businesses and households that provide food and the facilities and organizations that receive it. The benefit for providers is that they can reduce disposal costs. The benefit for recipients is that they can reduce food expenses. If food-bank activities become even more widespread, the amount of wasted food will decrease, and more people will be helped.

(Note 1) Damaged packaging: a condition in which a product's packaging has been torn.

(Note 2) Excess inventory: an excessive amount of stock being held.

(Note 3) Sell-by date and use-by date: the deadlines indicating when an item may still be sold and when it can still be eaten safely.
default.q.test-12-q3-3.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 商品の内容
From Text A, the reader knows that the product is「電動ランニングマシン」(an electric treadmill), allowing them to identify the contents of the item ordered and paid for by the customer.
default.q.test-12-q3-3.explanation: The decisive evidence is found in Text A: 「さて、1月15日付けで請求させていただきました「電動ランニングマシン」の代金につきましてお支払いいただき、誠にありがとうございます。」 (“We sincerely thank you for paying for the ‘electric treadmill’ for which we sent an invoice dated January 15.”). In formal business correspondence, 「N + につきまして」 attaches directly to a noun and introduces a topic or object in a formal, polite manner. Here, it clearly identifies the product involved in the transaction as 「電動ランニングマシン」 (“electric treadmill”). Text B only states that the company shipped the item by courier that day (本日、宅配便△△にて発送いたしました); it does not mention the date when it will reach the customer (到着日). The key strategy for N2 business-letter comparison questions is to avoid unsupported inferences: 「代金」 and the fact that payment was made provide only context, with no specific amount or payment method. Therefore, the only precisely identifiable information is the product content (商品の内容).
default.q.test-12-q3-3.why.0: ✓ (a) Passage A specifically names the item paid for as 「電動ランニングマシン」 (an electric treadmill).
default.q.test-12-q3-3.why.1: ✗ (b) Both texts mention only the date the notice was sent and the shipping date (本日発送いたしました); neither gives the delivery date.
default.q.test-12-q3-3.why.2: ✗ (c) The text only confirms that the customer has made the payment (お支払いいただき); it does not state the specific amount paid.
default.q.test-12-q3-3.why.3: ✗ (d) The passage does not mention any form of payment, such as a bank transfer, cash, or credit card.
default.q.test-13-q4-4.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 羽が退化していて飛べず、長距離移動ができないから。
The reason is that the wings of the Maimaikaburi beetle have degenerated, preventing it from flying long distances. This has led to geographic isolation and separate development in different regions.
default.q.test-13-q4-4.explanation: The direct evidence appears in the final part of the passage: 「これは、マイマイカブリの羽が退化していて、飛ぶことができないからだと考えられています。つまり、飛ぶことができないために長い距離を移動することができず、各地域でそれぞれ独自に分化していったというのです」 (This is thought to be because the wings of the Maimaikaburi beetle have degenerated, making it unable to fly. In other words, because it cannot fly, it cannot travel long distances, so it gradually differentiated independently in each region.) The objective-cause pattern 「V-ない＋ために」 (“because it cannot …”) combines with the explanatory conjunction 「つまり」 (“in other words”) and the reason pattern 「～からだ」 to clarify the direct causal relationship between the physical limitation and the separation of populations. The phenomenon is a gradual process of change over time caused by geographical isolation, expressed through the progressive form 「分化していった」 (“gradually differentiated”). In JLPT N2 questions asking for the reason (理由は何か), look for explanatory connectors such as 「～からだ」 and 「つまり」, and immediately eliminate unsupported inferences such as (c) or misleading claims about degree of ability such as (d).
default.q.test-13-q4-4.why.0: ✓ (a) This matches the passage exactly: the divergence was caused by their degenerated wings, which prevented them from flying and traveling far.
default.q.test-13-q4-4.why.1: ✗ (b) Incorrect because the passage states that this insect cannot fly to travel long distances, not that it moves back and forth between regions to find a suitable habitat.
default.q.test-13-q4-4.why.2: ✗ (c) The passage contains no information stating that their distinctive colors or shapes help them defend themselves against enemies and survive.
default.q.test-13-q4-4.why.3: ✗ (d) The entire species of insects has degenerated wings and lost the ability to fly; the issue is not a difference in flying ability among individual insects.
